newsitem.title: CANADA: Protectionism growing in G7, Canada poll finds.
newsitem.headline: Protectionism growing in G7, Canada poll finds.

text.p: Most people in the Group of Seven industrialized nations (G7) see protectionism rather than liberalized trade as the best route to national prosperity, according to an international survey released on Friday.

The poll by the Canada-based Angus Reid group, released as G7 leaders and Russian President Boris Yeltsin met in Denver for the annual summit of industrialized nations, showed a protectionist tide in four of the G7 countries surveyed.
A majority of respondents in the United States, Britain, France and Italy favored protectionist policies.
The survey showed 53 percent of Americans supporting protectionism, versus 41 percent backing freer trade.

"The United States, which has been one of the world's biggest free traders, now has a majority of the population wanting to close the borders," said Darrell Bricker, senior vice-president of public affairs with Angus Reid.
"That is really surprising when you consider how aggressive the U.S government has been in pursuing trade," Bricker said.
Among Canadians, 46 percent backed protectionism and 48 favored more liberalized trade.
Only Japan, Germany and Russia, which was included in the poll, showed a larger number of people supporting expanded trade.
Russians were the strongest supporters of liberalized trade, with 60 percent in favor. Fifty-nine percent of Japanese respondents supported liberalized trade, versus 37 percent for protectionism.
"The degree of diversity that exists on the issue of trade among the players at the table this weekend is really surprising," said Bricker.

The poll surveyed 3,207 people in eight countries in March. Canadian and U.S. samples had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percent, 19 times out of 20. The rest had a 7 percent margin of error 19 times out of 20.
Asked about the outlook for future generations, only American and British respondents agreed their children would be better off than they were.
Among Canadians, 53 percent thought their children faced a poorer future.
Eighty percent of Canadian respondents said opportunities for young people seemed to be getting bleaker.
Analysts said, however, that Canada's chronic unemployment, which has hovered around 10 percent for years, had colored the poll results.
